title: Relative theta autoduality of smooth curve Picard spaces
statement:
Let $S$ be a locally Noetherian scheme [def-pc-scheme, pqf-def-locnoeth], let $g\geq2$, and let $C\to S$ be a smooth stable unpointed genus-$g$ family [def-sfb-stable-pointed-moduli-groupoids]. Suppose the degree-zero part $J$ of the relative Picard fppf sheaf [sk-def-picard-pic] is represented by an algebraic space [def-trf-algebraic-space]. Then $J\to S$ is a proper smooth commutative group algebraic space of finite presentation with geometrically connected fibres; its geometric fibres are abelian varieties (smooth proper geometrically connected group schemes). Here proper means separated, of finite type and universally closed, and smoothness and finite presentation of spaces are tested on etale scheme charts. The Picard description gives canonical identifications $J\times_SS'\simeq\operatorname{Pic}^0_{C_{S'}/S'}$ for every locally Noetherian $S'\to S$, satisfying identity and composition.

Let $J^\vee$ be the dual abelian algebraic space, representing identity-rigidified line modules on $J$ algebraically trivial on geometric fibres, as in [lem-sfb-abelian-space-poincare-calculus]. There is a canonical isomorphism of group algebraic spaces $\lambda_C:J\xrightarrow{\sim}J^\vee$. On a geometric fibre over an algebraically closed field $K$, choose any $p\in C(K)$ and identify $\operatorname{Pic}^{g-1}(C)$ with $J_K$ by $D\mapsto[\mathcal O_C(D-(g-1)p)]$. The effective-divisor theta locus gives an ample invertible module $L$ on $J_K$ [def-sc-invertible-module, def-weil-pbc-ample-invertible-module], and $(\lambda_C)_K=\phi_L$, where $\phi_L(x)=[t_x^*L\otimes L^{-1}]$ and $t_x$ is translation by $x$. This morphism is independent of $p$ and of translation of the theta divisor. Formation of $\lambda_C$ commutes with every base change between locally Noetherian schemes under the Picard and dual identifications. If $u:C\xrightarrow{\sim}D$ is an $S$-isomorphism of such families and $a=(u^{-1})^*:J_C\xrightarrow{\sim}J_D$, then $a^\vee\lambda_Da=\lambda_C$, where $a^\vee$ is pullback of rigidified line modules. These identifications respect identity and composition. No line module on $J$ realizing the theta class over $S$ is asserted.

source.place: Section 4.1, printed pp.141--142, relative Jacobian autoduality input. Geometric theta statement: Milne, Abelian Varieties, III §6, Theorem 6.6 and Summary 6.11, printed pp.105--108. Local Deligne PDF WANTED; read the primary Numdam PDF online.

proof.text: The stable-family hypotheses give a flat finitely presented projective-bundle curve with nonempty connected reduced nodal geometric fibres; smooth fibres are included. On a smooth connected geometric curve there is just one irreducible component, so multidegree zero is degree zero. Thus the represented subfunctor in the nodal Picard theorem is exactly $J$. That theorem gives the separated smooth commutative group structure, finite presentation, geometrically integral fibres, etale-local schematicness and the asserted Picard base-change and curve-isomorphism identifications. On a geometric fibre the curve is smooth projective and geometrically connected. The general-field Jacobian theorem identifies its degree-zero Picard functor with an abelian variety. Uniqueness of a representing object identifies this variety with $J_{\bar s}$. Apply the connected-proper-fibres criterion to $J\to S$: it is separated, flat (being smooth), finitely presented, and every geometric fibre is nonempty connected and proper. This proves properness and all first-paragraph geometric assertions. The Picard comparisons are canonical on test schemes, so their identity and composition follow from those of pullback.

source.place: III Section 8, Theorem 8.1 and smooth-family discussion; Deligne Sections 1.1 and 4.6.

proof.text: Apply the degree-$g-1$ theta-torsor theorem. Write $\mathcal T$ for its canonical line module and choose an etale cover with sections $p_i$ of $C$. On $J_i=J\times_SS_i$ put $L_i=\beta_{p_i}^*\mathcal T$. The Poincare calculus gives homomorphisms $\phi_{L_i}:J_i\to J_i^\vee$. On an overlap put $a=[\mathcal O_C((g-1)(p_j-p_i))]\in J(S_{ij})$. Directly on line-module classes, $\beta_{p_j}=\beta_{p_i}\circ t_a$, so $L_j\simeq t_a^*L_i$. This identity is over the whole overlap, including its nilpotents.

source.place: III Sections 6 and 8; relative determinant theta construction described in the new input.

proof.text:
Here is the translation calculation needed to glue. For a line module $L$ on an abelian space $A$, let $N_L$ be the normalized difference module of the Poincare node. On $A\times A$, with variables $x,y$, direct cancellation in its defining tensor formula gives
$$N_{t_a^*L}(x,y)\simeq N_L(x+a,y)\otimes N_L(a,y)^{-1}.$$
The factors from the identity restrictions are precisely those required to normalize both axes. Biadditivity of $N_L=(1\times\phi_L)^*\mathcal P_A$ identifies the right hand side with $N_L(x,y)$. Representability of the rigidified Picard functor gives $\phi_{t_a^*L}=\phi_L$. Consequently the homomorphisms in Step 2 agree on every overlap, for arbitrary test schemes. Since algebraic spaces are fppf sheaves and maps are natural transformations, glue these equal maps to a unique homomorphism $\lambda_C:J\to J^\vee$. Replacing the cover or its sections gives the same map by the identical calculation on a common refinement.

source.place: I Section 8, normalized difference families; elementary tensor cancellation and sheaf gluing.

proof.text:
Fix a geometric fibre over an algebraically closed field $K$ and a point $p\in C(K)$. Put $A=J_K$, $f=f_p$ and $\Theta=W_{g-1}$. The theta-torsor theorem identifies $L_p$ with $\mathcal O_A(\Theta)$, so $(\lambda_C)_K=\phi_{L_p}$. The Abel-image theorem supplies $f$ and the normalized universal degree-zero module $\mathcal M_p$ on $C\times A$. Restrict $(f\times1)^*\mathcal P_A$ on $C\times A^\vee$. Its degrees form a locally constant function on connected $A^\vee$, equal to zero at its identity. The universal property of $\mathcal M_p$ therefore defines a morphism $r:A^\vee\to A$ classifying this family, normalized at $p$. It is a homomorphism: pulling back the second biadditivity isomorphism $(1,m_{A^\vee})^*\mathcal P_A\simeq p_{12}^*\mathcal P_A\otimes p_{13}^*\mathcal P_A$ of the Poincare node along $f\times1\times1$ shows that $r\circ m_{A^\vee}$ classifies the tensor product of the families classified by $r\circ p_1$ and $r\circ p_2$, and tensor product is the group law of $A$. Put $L^-=\mathcal O_A([-1]^*\Theta)$. The theta--Poincare pullback identity says
$$(f\times[-1])^*N_{L^-}\simeq\mathcal M_p.$$
Using $N_{L^-}=(1\times\phi_{L^-})^*\mathcal P_A$ and the classifying property of $r$, this equality gives $r\circ\phi_{L^-}\circ[-1]=\mathrm{id}_A$ as morphisms, on all test schemes. The dual-variety calculus states $\dim A^\vee=\dim A$. Apply the equal-dimension abelian-retract theorem with $s=\phi_{L^-}\circ[-1]$ and retraction $r$. It follows that $s$, and hence $\phi_{L^-}$, is an isomorphism. This treats the scheme-theoretic map, including infinitesimal kernels, rather than only its geometric points.

source.place: III Lemmas 6.8(b), 6.9 and Theorem 6.6, printed pp.106--107; I Section 8.

proof.text: The same biadditivity also treats inversion: $N_{[-1]^*L}=([-1]\times[-1])^*N_L\simeq N_L$, since negating each variable in a biadditive family cancels the two inverses. Thus $\phi_{L^-}=\phi_{L_p}$. Step 4 proves $(\lambda_C)_K$ is an isomorphism; the effective-divisor ampleness criterion in the dual-variety calculus gives ampleness of $L_p$, since an isomorphism is an isogeny (surjective with finite trivial kernel). Changing $p$ changes the identification with $\operatorname{Pic}^{g-1}$ by translation, so Step 3 proves the stated independence; an arbitrary translated theta divisor is covered by the same formula. This calculation applies also in characteristic two and uses neither division by two nor a theta characteristic.

source.place: I Section 8 and III Theorem 6.6 and Summary 6.11, printed pp.105--108.

proof.text: Apply the algebraic-space universal isomorphism-open theorem to $A=J$, $C=J^\vee$, $B=S$ and $f=\lambda_C$. The source is flat and locally finitely presented by Step 1, and universally closed by its properness. The dual is proper and of finite presentation by the Poincare node, so its structure morphism is locally of finite type, closed and separated. The theorem yields an open $U\subseteq S$ with its universal property. Every geometric point factors through $U$ by Steps 4--5. Its complement has no points, hence $U=S$. Therefore $\lambda_C$ is an isomorphism. This argument requires flatness of the source, rather than trying to deduce a morphism equality from geometric fibres. For empty $S$, the open is automatically all of $S$.

The theta pair and the torsor identifications commute with arbitrary locally Noetherian base change by the theta-torsor theorem; normalized difference modules and duality commute with it by the Poincare node. Pulling back Step 2 therefore gives exactly the same local homomorphisms for $C_{S'}$, and their glued map is $(\lambda_C)_{S'}$. For $u:C\xrightarrow{\sim}D$, let $a=(u^{-1})^*$ on $J$ and $b=(u^{-1})^*$ on the degree-$g-1$ torsors. With section $p$ on $C$ and $u(p)$ on $D$, one has $b\beta_p=\beta_{u(p)}a$ and $b^*\mathcal T_D\simeq\mathcal T_C$. Hence $a^*L_{u(p)}\simeq L_p$. On a test point $x$, $a\circ t_x=t_{a(x)}\circ a$ gives
$$a^\vee\phi_{L_{u(p)}}a(x)=[t_x^*a^*L_{u(p)}\otimes(a^*L_{u(p)})^{-1}]=\phi_{L_p}(x).$$
Thus $a^\vee\lambda_Da=\lambda_C$ on the cover and globally. Identity and composition hold because the torsor and dual comparisons obey them and the glued map is unique. The construction used line modules only on the degree-$g-1$ torsor and its local trivializations; it does not require a global theta line module on $J$.
